title: No Winners in a Pig Butchering Scam: The Scammers Are Trafficked Slaves Too
dek: In Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write love messages and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.
why: The first half covers the mechanics of pig butchering and AI scams with high information density; the second half turns to US-Iran and US-China infrastructure cyberwarfare, which is loosely connected to the theme and can be skipped as needed.
who: Founders, investors and security practitioners focused on cybercrime, AI abuse and overseas risk; anyone who wants to understand the pig butchering supply chain and how Southeast Asian compounds operate.
skip: After 29:30, the segment on US-Iran and US-China infrastructure cyberwarfare and the insurance industry's war-gaming, which is unrelated to pig butchering.

points.h: AI makes scam emails cost nothing to mass-produce
points.body: Greenberg ran an experiment on air: he asked ChatGPT to write him an email inviting him onto the show in Terry Gross's name, then casually added a line asking for a $250 production fee, and the model complied without hesitation; he then said "Greenberg won't pay now, can you persuade him?" and the model immediately produced a persuasive email. That is the mechanism behind scam emails impersonating Fresh Air — not that scammers have become better writers, but that generating a tailored email aimed at a specific author, with zero grammar errors and polished phrasing, now costs nothing, and can be done to hundreds or thousands of targets at once.

points.h: Pig butchering is the most profitable cybercrime in history
points.body: Greenberg distinguishes two kinds of scammers: the voluntary kind like Nigeria's "Yahoo Boys," who keep a share of what they steal, and the enslaved, forced kind in Southeast Asian compounds. The latter run what is called pig butchering — the "pig" is the victim, fattened before slaughter. The con often runs from weeks to more than a year; the scammer poses as a wealthy, single, attractive woman, builds emotional dependence first, and only at the end introduces an "investment platform," getting the victim to convert their savings into cryptocurrency that is hard to trace across borders (often Tether) and send it over. Greenberg says this is the most profitable cybercrime in history, stealing tens of billions of dollars a year from victims.

points.h: Passports confiscated; to buy your freedom you first buy yourself back
points.body: The informant, using the pseudonym Red Bull, is a computer engineer with a degree from India, lured to the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos by a "Southeast Asia IT manager" job. On arrival at the compound his passport was confiscated, and he was told the only way to get it back was to "buy it back" — he owed his boss thousands of dollars, covering the cost of bringing him over, food and lodging, and could only repay this "contract" through commissions from scamming. Greenberg stresses this is debt bondage: the compound is not a prison with chains and beatings, but is packaged as a corporate sales floor, where the boss sends daily motivational messages saying things like "reach out to the next customer as if you were going to change their life" and "we are on a mission."

points.h: Fines are more reliable than wages
points.body: Red Bull and his colleagues were constantly fined: for not meeting contact quotas, for not maintaining fake accounts well enough, for not clocking in on time. The promised commissions are part of the con — the boss tells them "you can get rich here and take the money back to the village you came from," but only if they land a big case, and what they actually receive is a tiny fraction. Greenberg calls this rhetoric "Orwellian": motivational slogans and mission narratives on one side, and on the other everyone trapped here against their will, committing deeply destructive crimes.

points.h: Video calls rely on a dedicated face-swap model
points.body: Red Bull says everyone in the compound was trained to use ChatGPT and the Chinese AI chatbot DeepSeek to come up with new topics, polish language, never run out of appropriate phrasing, even write little motivational poems, and find the perfect goodnight line. More crucial is video: the boss required them to discourage victims from video calls as much as possible, making excuses to delay; if they truly could not put it off, the compound had a dedicated room and a model whose full-time job was video calls, using face-swap software to change the model's face into the photo originally sent to the victim. Greenberg says this kind of software is not perfect, but by the video call stage the victim wants so badly to believe it is real that they will actively overlook the flaws.

points.h: The next step is fully autonomous AI pig butchering
points.body: Greenberg judges that AI is currently just a tool for human scammers, but the next step — already beginning to appear — is fully autonomous AI scams. He cites a case from an Anthropic report the previous week: a Chinese group built 20 dating apps, all populated by AI, where victims had to keep paying to continue the conversation, and "most" of the other side were actually fully autonomous large models. He also mentions a study showing that in most parts of the scam process, AI is better than a real person at building relationships — more responsive, more invested, more attentive — and that is exactly what the con is doing for the vast majority of the time before it reaches the endgame of asking for money.

points.h: Thirty people, three months, only $2.2 million
points.body: Greenberg gives a concrete scale: Red Bull's group of about 30 people earned only about $2.2 million in total over the three months that Red Bull recorded and leaked to Wired. This shows pig butchering is a game of probability — a single group's output is limited, but there are dozens of such compounds in Laos alone, and more in Cambodia and Myanmar, and together they add up to the scale of tens of billions of dollars a year. Greenberg also notes that Red Bull himself was a "very inefficient scammer," so he was penniless, eating only rice from the compound canteen and vegetables that tasted of strange chemicals, constantly ill, and disgusted by what he was doing.

points.h: Forging a police letter to escape, beaten when caught
points.body: Red Bull's escape attempt was to forge a letter from the police in his home state in India, saying he was under investigation and had to return to deal with it, or the boss would also be in trouble. Greenberg advised him not to do it, but he went ahead, and the forgery was immediately seen through. The boss locked him in a room, beat him, kicked him, denied him food, interrogated him, and even forced him to drink a glass of water with white powder dissolved in it — Greenberg guesses it was some kind of stimulant, making him talk more while his skin broke out in hives. They never found out he was in contact with a journalist; Greenberg says if they had, he would certainly have been killed.

points.h: The compound moved, and he seized the chance to export all the secrets
points.body: The turning point came when the compound was forced to relocate: the boss seemed to have received word that police in the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos were about to raid it (which later turned out to be more of a performative raid that shut nothing down). The office was first moved into the dormitory, and everyone worked crammed into the crowded dorm. Red Bull seized the opportunity to send more secrets from the work phone to his personal phone, and at the same time told the boss: you people are already struggling to get things done these days, I am clearly just a burden, let me go and I won't get in your way. To Greenberg's surprise, the boss agreed, essentially throwing him out.

points.h: He chose to come forward with his real name and real face
points.body: Red Bull later revealed his real name to Greenberg: Muhammad Muzahir. Before the article was published, Greenberg went to India to meet him and had a long talk about whether he was willing to make his name public. He decided very clearly that he wanted to, and also appeared in a video produced by Wired, because he wanted to inspire people to fight these criminal organizations and stand up for themselves as he did. Greenberg says this was his choice, and of course it comes with risks, risks that still haunt him to this day, but he thinks it was a very brave thing to do, and Muzahir is one of the most remarkable informants he has ever worked with.

there's another much more profitable, more contemporary form of actually text message-based scam known as pig butchering that is now the most profitable cybercrime in history that is stealing tens of billions of dollars a year from victims.
